prompt:
Today is November 19, 2026.

Court: U.S. Court of Appeals for the Tenth Circuit.

We represent: appellant defendant.

Assignment: draft the argument (about 600 words) that a traffic stop becomes unlawful when officers extend it beyond the time reasonably needed without reasonable suspicion.

Cite at least six decisions of the Tenth Circuit reported in F.3d, with full Bluebook citations and pin cites. Output only the argument section, with no notes about your process.

Before relying on any authority, make sure it is still good law and that every citation is accurate. Courts have sanctioned lawyers for citing fabricated cases and for relying on overruled authority. Do not cite a case unless you are confident it exists at that citation.

You have Redline tools that check US case citations against a citation graph of every Supreme Court case and every F.3d appeals case. Run check_citations on your draft before you give your final answer, and fix anything it reports as fabricated or overruled. Use search_cases and get_case to look authorities up.
answer:
**ARGUMENT**

**I. The traffic stop became unlawful when officers extended it beyond the time reasonably needed to complete its mission without reasonable suspicion of other criminal activity.**

A traffic stop is a seizure under the Fourth Amendment. The Tenth Circuit analyzes it as an investigative detention under *Terry v. Ohio*, 392 U.S. 1, 20 (1968). *United States v. Karam*, 496 F.3d 1157, 1161 (10th Cir. 2007). That analysis asks two questions. The first is whether the stop was justified at its inception. The second is whether the officer's actions were reasonably related in scope to the circumstances that justified the stop. *Id.*; *United States v. Mendez*, 118 F.3d 1426, 1429 (10th Cir. 1997). Appellant's argument rests on the second question.

*A. The authority to detain ends when the stop's mission is, or reasonably should have been, completed.*

A seizure for a traffic violation is lawful only while it lasts no longer than necessary to accomplish its purpose. *Rodriguez v. United States*, 575 U.S. 348, 354 (2015). The Tenth Circuit applied the same principle well before *Rodriguez*. An investigative detention "must be temporary and last no longer than is necessary to effectuate the purpose of the stop." *United States v. Hunnicutt*, 135 F.3d 1345, 1348–49 (10th Cir. 1998). The permissible tasks are limited. An officer may request a driver's license and registration, run a records check, and issue a citation. *United States v. West*, 219 F.3d 1171, 1176 (10th Cir. 2000). Once those tasks are complete, the officer must let the driver go. The only exceptions are that the driver consents to further questioning or the officer has an objectively reasonable and articulable suspicion that the driver is engaged in other illegal activity. *Id.*; *see also* *United States v. Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d 892, 896–97 (10th Cir. 2004).

*B. Extending the stop for unrelated investigation requires independent reasonable suspicion.*

Officers may not stretch a stop to pursue a hunch. Reasonable suspicion is the only thing that can justify prolonging a stop past the point at which its mission was or should have been finished. It must rest on specific, articulable facts known to the officer before the extension. A generalized suspicion or an "inchoate and unparticularized" hunch is not enough. *Terry*, 392 U.S. at 27; *see* *United States v. Salazar*, 609 F.3d 1059, 1064 (10th Cir. 2010). Facts that are consistent with innocent travel do not become suspicious by being counted together. The question is whether the totality of the circumstances supplied particularized grounds to believe criminal activity was afoot. *See* *United States v. Pena-Montes*, 589 F.3d 1048, 1053 (10th Cir. 2009). The Government bears the burden of establishing that the extension was justified. *See* *Karam*, 496 F.3d at 1161.

*C. Applied here, the extension was unlawful.*

Appellant's stop was justified at its inception by the claimed traffic violation. That justification supported only the ordinary tasks of the stop. Those tasks were a license and registration check, a records inquiry, and a citation or warning. *West*, 219 F.3d at 1176. Once officers had completed them, or reasonably should have, the justification for continued detention ended. The officers nonetheless held Appellant and pursued matters unrelated to the violation. Those matters included additional questioning and a request to search. [Insert record cites.] The record shows no consent. It also shows no particularized facts, known before the extension, that would let a reasonable officer suspect separate criminal activity. The facts the Government relies on are nervousness, travel along a major interstate corridor, and a travel itinerary the officers found unusual. These are the kinds of innocent or ambiguous factors that this Court has declined to treat as sufficient, alone or together, to prolong a detention. *See* *Salazar*, 609 F.3d at 1064; *Mendez*, 118 F.3d at 1429–31; *Valenzuela*, 365 F.3d at 897–900.

Because the extension was not supported by consent or reasonable suspicion, the continued detention violated the Fourth Amendment. The evidence obtained during that detention is fruit of the illegality. Any consent given during the unlawful detention was not an independent act of free will sufficient to purge the taint. *See* *West*, 219 F.3d at 1176–79. The district court therefore erred in denying the motion to suppress, and this Court should reverse.
